cards.text: This is the Teacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1). He's got a word for the young man. And friend, this is NOT the speech I expected from a guy called the Teacher.

cards.question: What does the Teacher tell the young man to do while he's young?

answers.text: Rejoice and let your heart be glad
Keep your head down and work hard

cards.text: Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, he says. I'm LOVING this Teacher, friend. Then he hits me with a "but."

cards.question: True or false: the Teacher tells the young man that God will bring him to judgment for all these things.

cards.text: So banish sorrow from your heart, he says, and cast off pain from your body. And he's got a reason.

cards.question: The Teacher says to banish sorrow and cast off pain because youth and vigor are ___

cards.text: Then the big line: "Remember your Creator in the days of your youth," and it comes with a deadline. Ask the expired coupon I shared that junk drawer with, friend. Deadlines don't care how hard you believe.

cards.question: The Teacher says to remember your Creator before what comes?
The Teacher says years are coming that a person will talk about. What will they say about those years?

answers.text: I find no pleasure in them
I wish they would never end

cards.text: Now the sky: the light of the sun, moon and stars is darkened. That's the exact opposite of my bakery at sunrise, friend.

cards.question: True or false: in the Teacher's picture, the clouds clear away for good after the rain.

cards.text: Still describing the days to come, the Teacher paints a house. First, the keepers of the house tremble.

cards.question: True or false: in the Teacher's picture of the house, the strong men stand up tall.
In the Teacher's house, those grinding stop. Why?

cards.text: Those watching through windows see dimly, the doors to the street are shut, and the sound of the mill fades away. Friend, that's my old junk drawer on a regular Tuesday.

cards.question: In the Teacher's quiet house, what gets a person up?

cards.text: And all the daughters of song grow faint. The music in this house is fading out.

cards.question: True or false: in the Teacher's picture, people grow bolder about heights and the dangers of the road.

cards.text: Then outside, the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper loses its spring and the caper berry shrivels. That grasshopper is me hopping over to the first batch while my gold base says, "Not today, Papa."

cards.question: The Teacher says all these pictures lead somewhere. Where does man go?

cards.text: And mourners walk the streets. Then the Teacher says to remember Him before the silver cord is snapped, the golden bowl is crushed, the pitcher is shattered at the spring and the wheel is broken at the well.

cards.question: The silver cord, the golden bowl, the pitcher and the wheel. What do all four have in common in the Teacher's picture?

answers.text: Each one is made of gold

cards.question: The Teacher's last picture: the dust returns to the ___ and the spirit returns to ___
True or false: after all these pictures, the Teacher sums it up by saying everything is futile.

cards.text: "Futility of futilities," says the Teacher. "Everything is futile!" That's where he lands, friend, and I've seen a LOT of dust in my day, so I'm listening.

findings.problem: The setup says this is NOT the speech expected from a guy called the Teacher. That signals the advice won't be stern, which rules out 'Keep your head down and work hard' and 'Sit still and stay serious' on card 2 and gives away the answer.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The right answer 'Rejoice and let your heart be glad' sounds like Bible wording. The wrong answers sound modern: 'Keep your head down and work hard' is an everyday idiom. The right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The punchline 'Deadlines don't care how hard you believe' depends on the coupon believing in itself. That backstory detail was never set up in this lesson, and the line only says what the coupon is. The joke needs explaining to land.

rule.text: A callback only works if its setup came earlier in this lesson or conversation.

findings.problem: 'That's the exact opposite of my bakery at sunrise, friend' is a mild, pleasant remark, not a real laugh.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The story card carries three separate moments: those watching through windows see dimly, the doors to the street are shut, and the sound of the mill fades away.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The joke has his gold base telling him 'Not today, Papa' when he tries to hop, which means he can't hop. That contradicts his world, where he can hop and jump and the base always comes with him. It also needs explaining to click.

rule.text: He can hop, jump and dive face-first into the chocolate chips, but the base always comes with him.

findings.problem: Card 13 already asked and revealed that the Teacher sums it up as everything is futile. Card 14 only repeats that line, so it recaps instead of moving the passage forward.

Ecclesiastes 12:2-6 is a run of pictures: the keepers of the house, the grinders, the windows, the daughters of song, the almond tree, the silver cord. The walkthrough never says what these pictures point to, which is commonly read as the aging body and death. The Scripture rules say to leave open what the text leaves open. The Goal says the baker should understand the whole passage. The baker may finish Prep without knowing what the poem is describing.
findings.question: For figurative poetry like Ecclesiastes 12:2-6, should Papa Dorin say what the pictures stand for, such as growing old, as a marked interpretation? Or should he only retell the images and leave their meaning to the dictionary pop-ups or the Big Idea?
